newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian MTBE - Extends gains amid healthy enquiries.
newsitem.headline: Asian MTBE - Extends gains amid healthy enquiries.

text.p: Asian MTBE prices extended their one-month gain, rising in the past week amid a tight market and healthy demand, traders said on Wednesday.
Sellers of the few parcels left in August said they were targetting at least $270 per tonne, free-on-board (fob) Singapore. Last Wednesday, fob prices were quoted between $263-$268.
"Buyers have no choice. They may indicate bids in the high $260s, but July is totally dry and August is quite fully booked," said one producer.
Prices were last assessed as high as $270 in early April, but fell as low as $245/$255 mid-May amid lacklustre demand in the region.
Since late June prices have been on the rise on the back of firmer prices in the U.S. and Europe and strong arbitrage demand.
Compared to the other regions, Asian MTBE prices are still the lowest and the arbitrage to the U.S. remains open at up to $280 per tonne, fob Singapore.
"U.S. demand in healthy. Cargoes from the Mideast and Asia -- South Korea and Malaysia -- have been moving to the U.S.," a producer said.
"There is sudden demand in the high-octane (gasoline) market and blenders and refiners are seeking MTBE," he said.
Demand for the octane-enhancer from gasoline blenders is re-emerged amid cuts in reformers in Singapore, some sources said.

Refiners in Singapore said reformer output has been cut as the cost of the feedstock naphtha is only around $1.50 per barrel lower than the high-octane gasoline produced. Normal break-even costs vary from $3 to $5.

Reflecting the firmer Singapore prices, Thai refiner Bangchak Petroleum Plc received much higher offers in its tender to buy 1,500 tonnes for delivery in August which closed on July 17 and was valid until July 18.
Due to a long weekend holiday in Thailand, Bangchak was still negotiating, but the best offer was heard aroud the high $270s on a cost-and-freight basis, up from its July award at $263, sources said.
Traders said they expected prices to firm further.
"It is firm and should be climbing," a trader said. "The whole of August in the Middle East is fully booked which is going to affect deliveries and supplies in Asia in September."
